messages.author: e174d246020b1d33
messages.subject: Reparameterizing hierarchical lifetime model
parts:
I am getting a few divergent transitions, which appear where the acceptance probability is below the median (lower diagonal of the pairs plot) and I have exhausted my knowledge of techniques to increase the numerical stability of my problem. Any suggestions?

The model consists of M distributions of the form F = 1 - (1 - pi * F_1) * (1 - F_2) where pi represents the probability that a unit is susceptible to a mechanism that results in "infant mortality". This is a competing risks model where we are agnostic about which failure mode was responsible for an observed failure.

The data we are modeling are either observed failures or right-censored and there is unit-specific left truncation. Because most observations are right-censored, we reparameterize in terms of a lower quantile rather than the mean of F_2.

//modified competing risk model

functions {
  real sev_logpdf(real y, real mu, real log_sigma){
    real z;
    z = (y - mu) / exp(log_sigma);
    return -log_sigma + z - exp(z);
  }
  
  real sev_logccdf(real y, real mu, real log_sigma){
    return -exp((y - mu) / exp(log_sigma));
  }
  
  real sev_logcdf(real y, real mu, real log_sigma){
    return log1m_exp(-exp((y - mu) / exp(log_sigma)));
  }
}

data {
  int M;
  int N_obs;
  int N_cens;
  real endtime_obs[N_obs];
  real endtime_cens[N_cens];
  real starttime_obs[N_obs];
  real starttime_cens[N_cens];
  int<lower=1, upper=M> dm_obs[N_obs];
  int<lower=1, upper=M> dm_cens[N_cens];
  vector<lower=0, upper=1>[2] p; # quantiles to model
}
transformed data{
  vector[2] z_corr;
  for(i in 1:2)
    z_corr[i] = log(-1.0 * log1m(p[i])); # used to get location(mu) from quantile(t_p)
}
parameters{
  real eta_ltp1; #locations
  real eta_ltp2;
  real eta_ls1;
  real eta_ls2;
  real eta_pi;
  real<lower=0> tau_ltp1; #scales
  real<lower=0> tau_ltp2;
  real<lower=0> tau_ls1;
  real<lower=0> tau_ls2;
  real<lower=0> tau_pi;
  vector[M] log_tp1_raw;
  vector[M] log_tp2_raw;
  vector[M] log_sigma1_raw;
  vector[M] log_sigma2_raw;
  vector[M] logit_pi_raw;
}

transformed parameters{
  vector[M] mu1;
  vector[M] mu2;
  vector[M] log_sigma1;
  vector[M] log_sigma2;
  vector[M] log_pi;
  log_sigma1 = eta_ls1 + tau_ls1 * log_sigma1_raw;
  log_sigma2 = eta_ls2 + tau_ls2 * log_sigma2_raw;
  mu1 = (eta_ltp1 + tau_ltp1 * log_tp1_raw) - (exp(log_sigma1) * z_corr[1]);
  mu2 = (eta_ltp2 + tau_ltp2 * log_tp2_raw) - (exp(log_sigma2) * z_corr[2]);
  for(m in 1:M)
    log_pi[m] = log_inv_logit(eta_pi + tau_pi * logit_pi_raw[m]);
}

model{
  real tmp[2];
  int m;
  real logpi;
  real mu_1;
  real mu_2;
  real ls_1;
  real ls_2;
  
  for(i in 1:N_obs){
    m = dm_obs[i];
    logpi = log_pi[m];
    mu_1 = mu1[m];
    mu_2 = mu2[m];
    ls_1 = log_sigma1[m];
    ls_2 = log_sigma2[m];
    // numerator:   log( p * f1 * (1 - F2) + f2 * (1 - p * F1) )
    //            = log( exp(log(p) + log(f1) + log(1 - F2)) + exp(log(f2) + log(1 - exp(log(p) + log(F1)))) )
    tmp[1] = log_sum_exp(logpi + sev_logpdf(endtime_obs[i], mu_1, ls_1) +
               sev_logccdf(endtime_obs[i], mu_2, ls_2),
               sev_logpdf( endtime_obs[i], mu_2, ls_2) + 
               log1m_exp(logpi + sev_logcdf(endtime_obs[i], mu_1, ls_1)
               )
             );
    // denominator:  log((1 - p * F1) * (1 - F2))
    //            =  log(1 - p * F1) + log(1 - F2)
    tmp[2] = log1m_exp(logpi + sev_logcdf(starttime_obs[i], mu_1, ls_1)) + 
             sev_logccdf(starttime_obs[i], mu_2, ls_2);
             
    target += tmp[1] - tmp[2];
  }
  
  for(i in 1:N_cens){
    m = dm_cens[i];
    logpi = log_pi[m];
    mu_1 = mu1[m];
    mu_2 = mu2[m];
    ls_1 = log_sigma1[m];
    ls_2 = log_sigma2[m];
  
    // numerator:   log((1 - p * F1) * (1 - F2))
    //            =  log(1 - p * F1) + log(1 - F2)
    tmp[1] = log1m_exp(logpi + sev_logcdf(endtime_cens[i], mu_1, ls_1)) + 
             sev_logccdf(endtime_cens[i], mu_2, ls_2);
    // denominator:  log((1 - p * F1) * (1 - F2))
    //            =  log(1 - p * F1) + log(1 - F2)
    tmp[2] = log1m_exp(logpi + sev_logcdf(starttime_cens[i], mu_1, ls_1)) + 
             sev_logccdf(starttime_cens[i], mu_2, ls_2);
             
    target += tmp[1] - tmp[2];
  }
  
  log_tp1_raw    ~ normal(0,1);
  log_tp2_raw    ~ normal(0,1);
  log_sigma1_raw ~ normal(0,1);
  log_sigma2_raw ~ normal(0,1);
  logit_pi_raw   ~ normal(0,1);
  eta_ltp1       ~ normal(7, 2);
  eta_ltp2       ~ normal(9, 2);
  eta_ls1        ~ normal(0, 1);
  eta_ls2        ~ normal(0, 1);
  eta_pi         ~ normal(-3, 1);
  tau_ltp1       ~ exponential(1);
  tau_ltp2       ~ exponential(1);
  tau_ls1        ~ exponential(1);
  tau_ls2        ~ exponential(1);
  tau_pi         ~ exponential(1);
}

You’ll definitely want to go through this implementation and make the
numerical calculations more robust.  For example, replace all of the
ratios of exponentials, exp(a) / exp(b), with a single exponential,
exp(a - b).

I am getting a few divergent transitions, which appear where the acceptance probability is below the median (lower diagonal of the pairs plot) and I have exhausted my knowledge of techniques to increase the numerical stability of my problem. Any suggestions?

  real tmp[2];

  real mu_1;

Thank you for the suggestion.

Are the edits below addressing that issue?

functions {
  real sev_logpdf(real y, real mu, real log_sigma){
    real z;
z = (y - mu) / exp(log_sigma); //  z = exp( log(y - mu) - log_sigma );

return -log_sigma + z - exp(z);
  }
  
  real sev_logccdf(real y, real mu, real log_sigma){
return -exp((y - mu) / exp(log_sigma)); // return -exp( exp ( log(y - mu) - log_sigma ) );

}

return log1m_exp(-exp((y - mu) / exp(log_sigma))); // return log1m_exp( -exp( exp ( log(y - mu) - log_sigma ) )

}


Are there any more specific issues related to numerical stability that stick out?

parts:
Those are nasty functions for numerical stability. exp()
is bad enough, but exp() inside of exp() is really nasty.
I just want to make sure that those are realy CCDFs on
the log scale. Because generally, the way to get stability
is to move to a lot scale.

Are you sure the divergences are post warmup? There was a bug
in reporting those in RStan, where warmup divergences were being
reported as post-warmup. That's fixed in the release about to come out.

- Bob

parts:
Those are nasty functions for numerical stability.  exp() 
is bad enough, but exp() inside of exp() is really nasty. 
I just want to make sure that those are realy CCDFs on 
the log scale.  Because generally, the way to get stability 
is to move to a lot scale.

Yes. The 'sev' distribution is a reflected Gumbel, so it does have a nested exponentiation. One of the "exp"s is there because I am modeling log(sigma). Alternatively, I could declare sigma > 0 in the parameters block and then use sigma ~ lognormal(eta_ls, tau_ls) (or some other distribution). I used the Matt trick for all of my group-level parameters, is that wrong-headed for scale parameters?

Are you sure the divergences are post warmup?  There was a bug 
in reporting those in RStan, where warmup divergences were being 
reported as post-warmup.  That's fixed in the release about to come out.
I saw something about that on here and I checked. They are post-warmup, happen sporadically, and they seem to be pretty evenly distributed across chains.
